To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the human brain can be considered as a complex system that can be modeled as a multi-dimensional dataset and that it can be characterized as a ‘fractal object’.

1) the number of independent sources that run in parallel in normal human brain is in the range 20-30 and 2) the number of ‘cpu cores’, i.e. the level of parallelization, increases with the complexity of the performed task.
the human brain can be treated as a ‘parallel processor’ with a number of ‘cpu cores’, and that this number can be estimated using fMRI data analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the human brain’s functional complexity and its parallel processing capacity, which is an important step towards understanding the brain’s functional architecture and its computational capabilities.
the estimation of the number of independent processes that are activated in parallel when the human brain performs complex cognitive tasks.
the estimation of the intrinsic dimensionality of fMRI data and the detection of the number of independent processes running in parallel when a specific activation threshold is defined.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in the human brain there is no fixed threshold for the number of ‘cpu cores’, but rather the level of parallelization is task-dependent and can vary from one to several hundreds of independent processes, which can be estimated via fractal analysis.

the number of ‘cpu cores’, or parallel brain processes, in the human brain is between 5 and 10 when a moderate to strong activation level (e.g., 5% to 10% of the brain) is defined, and that this number can be estimated via fMRI data analysis.
the human brain has a ‘cpu’ with a number of ‘cores’ that is proportional to the level of complexity of the task that the brain has to perform.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human brain can perform a specific cognitive task with the equivalent of 10-15 parallel processes.
the human brain is capable of performing a number of parallel processes that are proportional to the activation level.
, the human brain is a highly parallel processor with a very large degree of freedom, but with a limited capacity to process information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a single processor but a parallel processing system, and the number of parallel brain processes that can run simultaneously is limited to a specific range.
the brain activity can be treated as a multi-channel data space, which can be analyzed using data-driven methods, in order to extract the intrinsic properties of its complexity and dimensionality.
the human brain can perform complex tasks by utilizing a number of independent brain regions in parallel.
